Mobile Valeting vs a Local Car Wash: Is It Worth It?

By John Muriel20 September 20264 min read
Share
All articles

Mobile valeting typically costs more than a quick car wash because it takes longer, uses different products and tools, and comes to your home or workplace rather than you queuing up at a site. A car wash rinses off surface dirt in a few minutes; mobile valeting covers proper exterior and interior cleaning, done by hand, without the risk of the brushes and chemicals used at many drive-through washes. Whether the extra cost is worth it depends on how much you value your time and how thorough a clean you actually want.

It's a fair question, and one we get asked a lot — why pay more for someone to come to you when there's a car wash five minutes down the road? The honest answer is that they're not really the same service, even though both leave your car looking cleaner than before. Once you know what's actually different, it's a lot easier to decide which one makes sense for you.

What You're Actually Paying For

A car wash — whether it's an automatic tunnel or a hand wash site — is built around speed and volume. You drive in, it's done in minutes, you drive out. That's genuinely useful for a quick refresh between proper cleans.

Mobile valeting is a different model entirely. A valeter comes to your home or workplace with their own water, products, and equipment, and spends considerably longer on the car — properly washing, drying, and often covering the interior too. You're paying for their time, their travel, and the fact that you don't have to go anywhere or wait around.

Why Automatic Car Washes Can Actually Damage Paint

This is worth knowing regardless of which option you choose. Automatic car washes with rotating brushes reuse the same brushes on every car that passes through, picking up grit and dirt from previous vehicles. Over time, that causes fine scratching — the same swirl marks that a proper detail is trying to remove.

Touchless (chemical-only) automatic washes avoid the brush issue but rely on stronger detergents to shift dirt without contact, which can be harsher on wax, sealant, or ceramic coatings if the car goes through regularly.

None of this means car washes are bad — they're a useful, quick option. It just means they're not a substitute for a proper hand wash if you care about your paint condition long term.

What a Proper Mobile Valet Actually Includes

A genuine mobile valet, done properly, typically covers:

  • A two-bucket hand wash to avoid dragging dirt back across the paint
  • Wheels and arches cleaned separately from the bodywork (to avoid contaminating your wash mitt)
  • Proper drying with a clean microfibre towel or drying aid, rather than air-drying which causes water spotting
  • Interior vacuuming, wiping down, and glass cleaning
  • Tyre dressing and a final inspection

Compare that to a five-minute automatic wash, and the time difference alone explains most of the price gap.

When a Quick Car Wash Is the Right Call

There's no need to book a full valet every time your car gets a bit dusty. A car wash makes sense when:

  • You just need a quick refresh between proper valets
  • The car's genuinely not that dirty — light dust, a bit of road grime
  • You're short on time and it's a stopgap, not a replacement

When Mobile Valeting Is Worth the Extra Cost

Mobile valeting earns its price when:

  • You want the interior properly cleaned, not just the exterior
  • Your time is genuinely limited and the convenience of it coming to you matters
  • You've got a car with a wax, sealant, or ceramic coating you want maintained correctly, not stripped by harsh chemicals
  • You want a wash that won't add swirl marks to the paint

A Final Thought

Neither option is "better" in every situation — they're solving different problems. A car wash is a quick fix. Mobile valeting is a proper clean that protects your car's condition as well as its appearance, without you having to lift a finger or leave the house.

If you're not sure which your car actually needs right now, get in touch and we'll give you a straight answer, not just the most expensive option.

Is mobile valeting more expensive than a car wash?

Yes, typically. Mobile valeting takes longer, covers more of the car, and comes to you, which is reflected in the price compared to a quick automatic or hand car wash.

Can automatic car washes damage my car's paint?

Brush-based automatic washes reuse brushes across many vehicles, which can pick up grit and cause fine scratching over time. Touchless washes avoid this but use stronger chemicals instead.

What does a mobile valet actually include?

A proper mobile valet typically includes a two-bucket hand wash, separate wheel cleaning, careful drying, interior vacuuming and wiping, and a final inspection.

When is a quick car wash enough?

A car wash is fine for a quick refresh between proper valets, or when the car is only lightly dusty rather than genuinely dirty.

Does mobile valeting damage a wax or ceramic coating?

No, when done properly. A proper hand wash with the right products is gentler on existing coatings than harsh chemicals or brushes used at some automatic car washes.

7 Car Cleaning Myths That Are Damaging Your Paint

By John Muriel20 September 20264 min read
Share
All articles

Several widely believed car care habits actually damage paint over time — washing with dish soap, drying with a bath towel, and relying on automatic car washes are among the most common. These strip protective wax, introduce fine scratching, and speed up exactly the dulling most people are trying to avoid. None of them are obviously wrong at first glance, which is why they're so common.

Most people don't damage their car's paint on purpose — it happens through habits that seem completely reasonable, often passed down or just picked up along the way. We see the results of these regularly: paint that's been "looked after" for years but has more fine scratching than a car that's barely been washed at all. Here are the myths we come across most often, and what to do instead.

Myth 1: "Any washing-up liquid works fine"

Dish soap is designed to strip grease, which is exactly what it does to your car's wax or sealant layer too. Strip that protective layer often enough and the paint underneath is left more exposed to UV damage, contaminants, and the fine scratching that comes from washing without it. A pH-balanced car shampoo cleans without stripping that protection.

Myth 2: "Any towel will do for drying"

An old bath towel feels soft, but it's nowhere near as smooth as a proper microfibre drying towel at a microscopic level. Rough fibres dragged across paint while drying are a direct cause of fine scratching — ironically, often introduced at the exact moment you're trying to make the car look its best.

Myth 3: "Automatic car washes are basically the same as a hand wash"

Brush-based automatic washes reuse the same brushes across every car that passes through, picking up grit from previous vehicles along the way. That grit gets dragged across your paint on every visit. Touchless washes avoid the brush contact but often use stronger chemicals to compensate, which isn't necessarily gentler if a wax or coating is applied.

Myth 4: "Waxing once a year is plenty"

Wax and sealants wear away with washing, weather, and UV exposure — most last a matter of months, not a year. A car that's "waxed" but hasn't been topped up in months is often running with little to no actual protection left, even though it still looks fine on the surface.

Myth 5: "If it's shiny, the paint's healthy"

Shine can come from a fresh wash, a quick detailing spray, or even just water beading — none of which tell you anything about the condition of the clear coat underneath. Genuinely healthy paint holds up under close inspection in direct sunlight; a quick shine after a wash doesn't confirm that.

Myth 6: "Wiping off dust is fine if you're careful"

Dry-wiping dust off paint, even gently, drags whatever grit is sitting on the surface across the clear coat. It feels harmless because there's no visible mark afterwards, but this is one of the most common causes of the fine swirling that shows up later in direct light.

Myth 7: "Letting the car air-dry is easier and just as good"

Air-drying leaves mineral deposits from the water itself on the paint as it evaporates — water spots. Left long enough, especially in hard water areas, these can etch into the clear coat rather than just sitting on top, which is a lot harder to correct than simply drying the car properly in the first place.

A Final Thought

None of these habits are dramatic on their own — that's exactly why they're so widespread. It's the accumulation over months and years that leaves paint looking tired well before it should. Swapping to the right products and a proper drying method costs nothing extra and makes a genuine difference to how paint holds up over time.

If your car's paint already shows the effects of some of these habits, a machine polish can usually bring it back — get in touch and we'll take an honest look.

How to Care for Leather Car Seats (Without Ruining Them)

By John Muriel20 September 20264 min read
Share
All articles

Leather car seats need regular conditioning, not just cleaning, because everyday use, sunlight, and heat gradually dry out the leather's natural oils. Left untreated, this leads to cracking and premature ageing. The most common mistake owners make is using generic household cleaners or too much water, both of which can strip the leather's finish and cause staining rather than protecting it.

Leather seats are one of the first things people notice about a car's interior, and one of the first things that show neglect. Unlike fabric, leather isn't just something you wipe clean — it's a material that needs ongoing care to stay in good condition, and a lot of the damage we see could have been avoided with the right routine from the start.

Why Leather Needs Conditioning, Not Just Cleaning

Leather is a natural material that relies on its own oils to stay supple. Sunlight through the windscreen, heat from parked cars in summer, and simple day-to-day contact gradually dry those oils out. Once that happens, the leather becomes stiffer and more prone to cracking, particularly along seams and high-contact areas like the driver's seat bolster.

Cleaning removes dirt and surface grime, but it doesn't replace lost moisture. Conditioning is a separate step that restores flexibility and helps prevent the cracking that's very difficult to reverse once it's set in.

Common Mistakes That Damage Leather

A few habits we see regularly that do more harm than good:

  • Using household surface cleaners or baby wipes — many contain alcohol or harsh chemicals not designed for leather, which can strip its protective finish
  • Soaking the leather with too much water — leather absorbs moisture, and over-wetting can cause staining, especially on lighter colours
  • Skipping conditioning entirely — cleaning alone, done repeatedly without conditioning, gradually dries the leather out faster
  • Using the wrong products on perforated or aniline leather — some leather types are more delicate and need specific, gentler products; using a general-purpose cleaner on these can cause visible damage

A Simple Maintenance Routine

You don't need to overhaul your routine to keep leather in good condition — small, regular steps go a long way:

  • 1. Wipe down monthly with a dedicated leather cleaner and a soft microfibre cloth
  • 2. Condition every few months, more often in summer when heat exposure is higher
  • 3. Keep the car out of direct sun where possible, or use a windscreen shade, since UV exposure is one of the biggest causes of drying and fading
  • 4. Deal with spills straight away — the longer a spill sits, the more likely it is to stain

How to Spot Early Damage

Catching leather damage early makes a real difference to how well it can be treated. Watch for:

  • Slight stiffness or a papery feel compared to the rest of the seat
  • Fine surface cracking, often starting on the bolsters or high-wear areas
  • Colour fading, particularly on seats that get regular direct sunlight
  • A dull, matte appearance where the leather used to have a slight sheen

Any of these are signs the leather needs conditioning sooner rather than later — waiting usually means more extensive (and more expensive) restoration later on.

When It's Time to Call in a Professional

A home routine handles day-to-day maintenance well, but professional interior detailing is worth considering if:

  • The leather already shows visible cracking or significant dryness
  • There are stains that haven't shifted with regular cleaning
  • You're preparing the car for sale and want the interior presenting at its best
  • It's been a long time since the leather has had a proper deep clean and condition, rather than just a quick wipe

A Final Thought

Leather seats age well when they're looked after consistently, and age badly, fast, when they're not. A simple routine of the right cleaner and regular conditioning is genuinely all it takes to avoid the cracking and fading that's much harder to fix once it's happened.

If your leather's already showing signs of wear, get in touch — a proper deep clean and condition can often bring it back further than you'd expect.

Every few months is a reasonable guide, more often in summer when heat exposure is higher.

Slight stiffness, fine surface cracking on high-wear areas, colour fading, and a dull, matte appearance are common early signs.

End of Lease Car Prep: What Actually Needs Doing

By John Muriel20 September 20264 min read
Share
All articles

Lease companies assess returned cars against "fair wear and tear" standards, and the most common charges come from scuffed alloys, interior stains, and light exterior scratches. A pre-return valet and light paint correction, done a week or two before handback, can genuinely reduce or avoid these charges. It won't fix everything, though — dents, cracked glass, and major scratches are outside what detailing can address.

If you're coming to the end of a lease, the inspection at handback can be the difference between a clean handover and an unexpected bill. Most of what gets charged for is avoidable, or at least reducible, with the right prep beforehand — but timing and realistic expectations both matter here.

What Lease Companies Actually Check For

Handback inspections typically focus on:

  • Alloy wheels — kerb scuffs and scratches are one of the most commonly charged items
  • Interior condition — stains, odours, and excessive wear on seats and carpets
  • Exterior paintwork — scratches, chips, and dents beyond a certain size or number
  • Glass — chips or cracks in the windscreen
  • Tyres — tread depth below the required minimum
  • Missing items — spare keys, manuals, locking wheel nuts

Most inspection standards (commonly based on the BVRLA fair wear and tear guide) allow for a reasonable level of cosmetic wear given the car's age and mileage. The charges tend to come from wear beyond that reasonable threshold.

Fair Wear and Tear vs Chargeable Damage

This distinction matters, because not everything gets charged. Fair wear and tear generally covers:

  • Light scuffing consistent with normal use
  • Minor stone chips on the front of the car
  • General interior wear appropriate to the car's age and mileage

Chargeable damage tends to include:

  • Scratches or dents beyond a certain size, or in clusters
  • Stained or heavily soiled interior trim
  • Alloy wheel damage beyond light scuffing
  • Odours (smoke, pets) that require specialist treatment to remove

A pre-return detail is aimed squarely at the second category — bringing the car back down to what's reasonably expected, rather than trying to make it look brand new.

What a Pre-Return Detail Should Include

For most leased cars, a sensible pre-return prep covers:

  • Full interior deep clean — carpets, seats, and boot, addressing any stains or odours
  • Alloy wheel cleaning and light cosmetic touch-up where scuffing is only surface-level
  • Exterior wash and light paint correction on visible swirl marks or light scratching, where machine polishing can realistically improve the finish
  • Engine bay clean, if it's part of the inspection criteria (check your lease terms)
  • A final check against the handback checklist your leasing company provides, if you have one

What It Won't Fix

It's worth being upfront about the limits here, because a detail isn't a repair service:

  • Dents — these need paintless dent removal or bodywork, not detailing
  • Cracked or chipped glass — a windscreen repair or replacement is a separate job
  • Deep scratches through the clear coat — polishing removes fine scratching, not damage that's gone through to the colour coat
  • Alloy wheel damage beyond light scuffing — kerbed alloys with visible gouges usually need wheel refurbishment, not just cleaning

If your car has any of these, it's worth getting a separate repair quote alongside the detailing — sorting both before handback is usually far cheaper than the charges applied afterward.

Timing: Why Leaving It Too Late Costs More

Booking a valet the day before handback rarely gives enough time to properly assess and address everything. Stains need time to be treated properly, and if any repair work turns out to be needed (a chip, a dent), there often isn't time to arrange it. Booking a detail one to two weeks before your return date gives enough breathing room to catch and deal with anything that needs more than a clean.

A Final Thought

A proper pre-return detail is one of the more cost-effective things you can do before handing a leased car back — it directly targets the areas inspectors focus on, without you needing to guess what will or won't get charged. It won't turn back the clock on real damage, but for the wear and tear that builds up over a lease term, it makes a genuine difference.

If you've got a handback date coming up, get in touch — we can talk through what your car needs and the best timing to book it in.

Inspections typically focus on alloy wheels, interior condition, exterior paintwork, glass, tyres, and included items like spare keys.

What's the difference between fair wear and tear and chargeable damage?

Fair wear and tear covers light, age-appropriate cosmetic wear. Chargeable damage includes larger scratches, dents, stains, or wheel damage beyond light scuffing.

Will a valet fix a dent or cracked windscreen before handback?

No. Detailing addresses cleaning and light paint correction; dents and glass damage need separate repair services.

One to two weeks before your return date, to allow time for proper treatment and to arrange any separate repairs if needed.

Convertible Roof Cleaning: What Most Valets Get Wrong

By John Muriel20 September 20264 min read
Share
All articles

Soft-top roofs, whether fabric or vinyl, need different products and techniques to the rest of the car's bodywork. Standard car shampoo, pressure washing, or the wrong brush can strip the roof's waterproofing and cause it to crack or leak over time. Most general valets treat the roof the same as the paintwork, which is the main reason convertible owners end up with reduced water resistance or premature wear.

Convertible owners often assume their roof is being properly looked after as part of a standard valet, because it looks fine afterwards. The problem is that roof damage from the wrong products or technique doesn't usually show up immediately — it shows up months later as leaks, staining, or cracking, by which point it's a lot harder to fix than it would have been to simply do it right the first time.

Why Convertible Roofs Need Different Treatment to Paintwork

A car's bodywork is hard, non-porous paint with a clear coat. A convertible roof is a soft, often porous material designed to flex and seal against water — which means it reacts completely differently to washing.

Pressure washing, aggressive brushes, or high-alkaline shampoos designed for paint can strip the roof's waterproof coating, force water into stitching and seams, or cause premature fading and stiffening of the material. None of this is obvious straight after a wash — the damage builds up over repeated washes.

Fabric vs Vinyl Roofs — Different Care Needs

  • Fabric roofs (canvas-style) are porous and rely on an applied waterproof coating that wears down over time with washing, sun exposure, and general use. They need gentle, roof-specific cleaners and periodic re-proofing to maintain water resistance.
  • Vinyl roofs are less porous but can still crack or fade with harsh chemicals or prolonged UV exposure. They generally need a dedicated vinyl-safe cleaner and protectant rather than an all-purpose shampoo.

Using the wrong product type on either can strip existing protection rather than adding to it — worth checking with whoever's valeting the car that they know which type yours is.

Common Mistakes That Damage Waterproofing

  • Using standard car shampoo — many are too alkaline for roof fabric and strip factory waterproofing
  • Pressure washing directly onto the roof — can force water into seams and stitching, and may damage the coating outright
  • Scrubbing with a stiff brush — roof fabric is more delicate than paintwork and can be damaged by brushes fine for bodywork
  • Skipping re-proofing — even with gentle cleaning, waterproof coatings wear down and need reapplying periodically; without this, water resistance gradually declines regardless of how carefully it's washed

What Proper Roof Cleaning and Re-Proofing Involves

  • A dedicated roof-safe cleaner, applied by hand with a soft brush designed for fabric or vinyl roofs
  • Gentle rinsing, avoiding high-pressure water directly on seams
  • Full drying before any protectant is applied — trapping moisture under a fresh coating can cause its own problems
  • A roof-specific waterproofing protectant, reapplied periodically (typically every few months to a year, depending on use and weather exposure)

How Often It Should Be Done

Roof cleaning itself can be done as part of a normal wash routine, as long as the right products are used. Re-proofing (reapplying the waterproof coating) is generally needed less often — usually once or twice a year for regularly used convertibles, more frequently if the car's kept outside year-round rather than garaged.

A Final Thought

A convertible roof is one of the easiest parts of the car to damage without realising it, simply because the wrong products don't cause visible problems straight away. If your roof hasn't been treated with dedicated products in a while, it's worth checking its water resistance before the next wet spell catches you out.

If you're not sure what condition your roof's waterproofing is in, get in touch — we can take a look and advise honestly on what it needs.

Fabric roofs are porous and need gentle, roof-specific cleaners with periodic re-proofing, while vinyl roofs need a vinyl-safe cleaner and protectant.

A standard vacuum lifts loose pet hair but leaves behind hair that's woven into carpet fibres and seat fabric, which is most of it. Rubber-tipped tools, dampened gloves, or a proper extraction machine actually pull embedded hair out rather than just skimming the surface. That difference is why "vacuumed" and "pet hair removed" often describe two noticeably different results.

If you've ever vacuumed your car after a trip with the dog and still found hair everywhere a few days later, you're not doing anything wrong — a normal household or car vacuum just isn't built to shift hair that's worked its way into fabric weave. Here's why that happens, and what actually gets it out properly.

Why a Normal Vacuum Isn't Enough

Pet hair, especially from dogs and cats with fine undercoats, doesn't just sit on top of carpet and fabric — it works its way into the weave, held in place by static and the natural texture of the material. A standard vacuum nozzle pulls air and loose debris upward, but it doesn't have the friction or agitation needed to dislodge hair that's genuinely embedded. That's why repeated vacuuming often barely makes a dent.

What Actually Works

A few tools and techniques genuinely shift embedded hair, rather than just the loose surface layer:

  • Rubber-tipped brushes or pet hair tools — the rubber creates friction and static that lifts embedded hair to the surface, where it can then be vacuumed properly
  • Dampened rubber gloves — running a slightly damp rubber glove across seats or carpet bunches hair together, making it far easier to lift by hand or vacuum afterward
  • Lint rollers — effective on smaller, flatter areas like seat backs, less practical for carpet
  • Professional extraction equipment — combines suction with water and agitation, which is generally the most thorough option for carpets and heavily affected areas

Fabric vs Leather Seats — Different Approaches

  • Fabric seats hold hair the most stubbornly, since the woven texture traps it. Rubber tools and extraction work best here.
  • Leather seats don't trap hair the same way — a damp microfibre cloth or a soft brush is usually enough, and it's worth avoiding stiff-bristled brushes that can scratch the leather surface.

Keeping It Under Control Between Details

A few habits make a noticeable difference between proper cleans:

  • Use a seat cover or dedicated pet blanket for regular trips, rather than letting pets sit directly on fabric seats
  • Brush your pet before car journeys where possible, to reduce loose hair shedding in the first place
  • Quick rubber-glove pass after each trip, even without a full vacuum, keeps hair from building up and becoming more embedded over time

What to Ask a Valeter If Pet Hair Is Your Main Issue

If pet hair is the main thing bothering you about your car's interior, it's worth asking directly whether the valet includes proper pet hair removal tools and extraction, rather than assuming a standard interior clean will fully cover it. A general vacuum-and-wipe service and a dedicated pet hair treatment aren't always the same job, even though both get described as "interior cleaning."

A Final Thought

Pet hair is one of those things that feels like it should be simple to deal with, but genuinely needs the right tools to shift properly. A normal vacuum will always leave some behind if the hair's had time to embed — it's not a sign you're doing anything wrong, just a limitation of the tool.

If pet hair's become a losing battle in your car, get in touch — proper extraction makes a bigger difference than most people expect.

Rubber-tipped brushes, dampened rubber gloves, and professional extraction equipment are effective at lifting embedded hair.

Water Log Detailing: What It Is and When You Need It

By John Muriel20 September 20265 min read
Share
All articles

Water log detailing refers to deep-cleaning a car's interior after prolonged exposure to standing water — flooded footwells, waterlogged carpets, or a car left exposed to heavy rain through a leak. It's a bigger job than a normal interior clean because trapped water causes mould, corrosion, and lingering odour if it isn't fully extracted and properly dried out, rather than just wiped over on the surface.

Most interior detailing deals with dirt, dust, and general wear. Water logging is a different problem entirely — it usually happens suddenly (a leak, a flood, a window left open in heavy rain) and needs a faster, more thorough response than routine cleaning. Left too long, it stops being a cleaning job and starts becoming a genuine mechanical and structural concern.

What Counts as "Water Logged"

This covers more situations than people often expect:

  • A leaking door, window, or sunroof seal letting water in gradually over repeated rain
  • A blocked drain (pollen filter or sunroof) causing water to pool inside rather than draining away
  • A window left open during heavy rain, soaking seats and carpet directly
  • Flooding — standing water reaching the footwells or higher, whether from a storm, a burst pipe nearby, or driving through deep water
  • A significant spill — less common, but a large spilled drink or a leaking water container can waterlog carpet in a localised area

The key difference from a normal spill is volume and how long the water's been sitting — genuine water logging means carpet, underlay, and sometimes the cabin filter or wiring have been properly soaked, not just damp.

Why It's a Bigger Job Than a Standard Interior Valet

A standard interior valet is built around dirt and general wear — vacuuming, wiping, light stain treatment. Water logging introduces a few extra problems:

  • Underlay saturation — carpet underlay can hold water long after the visible carpet feels dry, continuing to cause damp and odour from underneath
  • Mould risk — standing water is exactly the environment mould needs, and it can start developing within 24–48 hours in the right conditions
  • Electrical risk — footwell flooding can reach wiring looms and connectors under the carpet, which is a genuine safety concern, not just a cleaning one
  • Corrosion — metal components under carpet and seats can start corroding if left wet for extended periods

A normal vacuum and wipe-down doesn't address any of these — it just cleans the visible surface while the underlying problem continues.

What Proper Water Extraction and Drying Involves

  • Full removal of standing water using wet-vacuum extraction equipment, not just towels or a standard vacuum
  • Lifting carpet where necessary to check and dry the underlay properly, rather than assuming the surface being dry means the job's done
  • Controlled drying — often using air movers or dehumidifiers to fully dry the interior over a period of time, rather than just leaving windows open
  • Antibacterial and antimicrobial treatment to address any mould or bacteria that's already started developing
  • Odour treatment once everything is genuinely dry, not before — treating a still-damp interior just masks the smell temporarily

Warning Signs You've Left It Too Long

  • A persistent musty smell that doesn't shift with normal cleaning or air fresheners
  • Visible mould spots on carpet, seat bases, or door cards
  • Electrical faults — flickering interior lights, a warning light that won't clear, or accessories behaving oddly
  • Carpet that still feels damp days after the water exposure, even if the surface looks dry

If you're seeing any of the electrical symptoms, it's worth getting the car checked by a mechanic alongside any detailing work, since water reaching wiring is a genuine safety issue.

What to Do Immediately If Your Car Floods

Before you can get it professionally treated:

  • 1. Remove as much standing water as possible — towels, a wet-vacuum if you have access to one, anything that shifts bulk water quickly
  • 2. Get air moving through the car — open windows and doors where weather allows, to start the drying process
  • 3. Avoid running electrics if water has clearly reached the footwells, until a mechanic has checked things over
  • 4. Book a proper water log detail as soon as possible — the longer standing water sits, the more likely mould and odour become, and the harder both are to fully remove

A Final Thought

Water logging is one of the more serious things that can happen to a car's interior, and it's not something a normal valet is built to handle properly. Acting quickly makes a genuine difference to the outcome — the gap between "fully recoverable" and "permanent odour and damage" often comes down to how fast it's dealt with.

If your car's been flooded or exposed to standing water, get in touch as soon as you can — we'll talk you through what needs doing and how urgently.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as a waterlogged car interior?

Situations like a leaking seal, a blocked drain, a window left open in heavy rain, or flooding reaching the footwells all count as water logging.

Why is water log detailing different from a normal interior clean?

Standing water can saturate carpet underlay, encourage mould growth, and even affect wiring, none of which a standard vacuum and wipe addresses.

How quickly can mould develop in a wet car interior?

Mould can start developing within 24 to 48 hours in the right conditions, so quick action matters.

What should I do immediately if my car floods?

Remove as much standing water as possible, get air moving through the car, avoid running electrics if the footwells are wet, and book a proper water log detail as soon as possible.

Can a waterlogged car cause electrical problems?

Yes, water reaching wiring under the carpet is a genuine safety concern and should be checked by a mechanic alongside any detailing work.

How Often Should You Actually Wash Your Car?

By John Muriel20 September 20264 min read
Share
All articles

Most cars benefit from a wash every one to two weeks, though the right frequency depends heavily on how and where you park and drive. Coastal areas, salted winter roads, tree sap, and bird droppings can all shorten that window considerably. Washing too infrequently lets contaminants bond to the paint over time, while washing incorrectly — wrong products, dirty tools — can cause more damage than simply not washing as often.

There's no single right answer here, despite how often the question gets asked as if there is one. The honest answer is "it depends," but there are clear factors that shift the right frequency for your specific car and circumstances, and a few genuine warning signs that tell you when you're overdue.

The General Rule of Thumb, and Why It Varies

Every one to two weeks is a reasonable baseline for most cars in typical UK conditions. That said, this is a starting point, not a fixed rule — a car parked under trees in a high-pollen area, or one driven daily on salted winter roads, needs washing more often than a car kept in a garage and driven occasionally.

Factors That Mean You Should Wash More Often

  • Coastal areas — salt air accelerates corrosion and leaves a residue on paint faster than inland areas
  • Winter road salt — one of the most corrosive substances your car regularly comes into contact with; more frequent washing, particularly of the underside, matters more in winter than any other season
  • Parking under trees — sap, pollen, and bird droppings are all genuinely damaging to paint if left to sit, and can etch into the clear coat over time
  • High-mileage or daily driving — simply more exposure to road grime, bugs, and general contamination
  • Light-coloured or dark-coloured paint that shows dirt easily — not a paint health issue, but a reasonable factor if appearance matters to you day to day

Signs You're Overdue a Wash

  • Dirt or grime that no longer wipes off easily with a light touch
  • Visible bird droppings, tree sap, or bug residue that's been sitting for more than a day or two
  • A noticeably duller appearance compared to how the paint normally looks after a wash
  • Reduced water beading, if your car has a wax, sealant, or ceramic coating — this is a sign contamination is starting to sit on top of the protective layer rather than beading off

Can You Wash Your Car "Too Much"?

Only if it's done incorrectly. Washing itself isn't harmful — what causes damage is the method: dirty wash mitts, the wrong products, or automatic car washes with brushes that introduce fine scratching. A car washed frequently but properly (two-bucket method, clean tools, appropriate products) will generally hold its paint condition better than one washed rarely but with the wrong technique.

How a Ceramic Coating Changes the Answer

A ceramic coating doesn't reduce how often a car needs washing in terms of keeping contaminants off the paint, but it does make each wash easier and generally more effective — dirt and grime don't bond to the surface as readily, so a coated car often comes clean with less effort and less risk of introducing scratches during the wash itself. It's a change in how easy washing is, more than how often it's needed.

A Final Thought

There's no perfect number that applies to every car — the right frequency comes down to where and how you drive, and how quickly contamination tends to build up on your specific car. The more useful habit is paying attention to the signs above rather than following a fixed schedule regardless of conditions.

If your car's paint isn't holding up the way it used to between washes, get in touch — it might be down to technique, condition, or simply time for a proper correction and protective coating.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I wash my car?

Every one to two weeks is a reasonable baseline for most cars, though it depends on how and where you drive and park.

Does living near the coast mean I should wash my car more often?

Yes, salt air accelerates corrosion and leaves residue on paint faster than inland areas, so more frequent washing helps.

Can washing my car too often damage the paint?

Only if done incorrectly. Frequent washing with the right technique and products is generally better for paint than infrequent washing.

Does a ceramic coating mean I need to wash my car less often?

Not necessarily less often, but each wash becomes easier and lower-risk, since dirt doesn't bond to the surface as readily.

What are the signs my car is overdue a wash?

Grime that doesn't wipe off easily, visible bird droppings or sap sitting for days, dullness, and reduced water beading on coated cars are all signs.

Everything in the Used Car Fresh Start Valet

A forecourt clean is built for speed. It makes a car look ready to sell, but it does not lift what has settled into the fabric over years of someone else's use. Seats, carpets, seatbelts, vents and the steering wheel are the places dirt, bacteria and old smells actually live, and they are the places a quick wash leaves alone.

That is the difference here. We treat the car as though it is starting again: every surface cleaned properly, the cabin steam sanitised, and any lingering smell traced back to its source rather than covered with fragrance. Everything else we use is eco-friendly and biodegradable, and our low-water method means we can work at your home or workplace without a hose or a drain.

Most used car deep cleans take 2 to 4 hours, depending on the size of the car and the state it arrived in. Heavy smoke can occasionally need a second treatment, and we will tell you that up front rather than after the fact.

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 29 September 2026

This policy explains how Ecoverde Valeting & Detailing Service ("Ecoverde", "we", "us") collects and uses your personal data when you visit our website, book a valet or contact us. We keep things simple: we only collect what we need to look after you and your car.

1. Who we are

Ecoverde Valeting & Detailing Service is a mobile car valeting and detailing business run by John Muriel as a sole trader. We serve West London, including Brentford (TW8), Ladbroke Grove (W10), Chiswick, Hammersmith, Ealing, Kew, Richmond, Notting Hill, Chelsea and Wimbledon.

For data protection purposes, John Muriel is the data controller.

  • Website: ecoverdevaleting.co.uk
  • Email: info@ecoverdevaleting.co.uk
  • Phone (Ladbroke Grove W10): 07871 553827
  • Phone (Brentford TW8): 07495 400369
  • WhatsApp: 07495 400369
  • Postal address: 87 West Row, Ladbroke Grove, London W10 5AX

2. What information we collect

When you book or contact us, we may collect:

  • Your name, phone number and email address
  • The address where you would like us to clean your car
  • Your vehicle details, such as make, model, colour and registration number
  • Booking details, such as the service you choose, date, time and any notes you give us
  • Payment details (these are handled by our payment provider, not stored by us)
  • Photos of your vehicle taken before and after our work
  • Messages you send us by email, phone, text, WhatsApp or social media

When you visit our website, we may also collect basic technical data, such as your IP address, browser type and the pages you visit. This is collected through cookies (see section 8).

3. How we use your information

We use your information to:

  • Take, confirm and manage your booking
  • Find your car and carry out the service
  • Take payment and send receipts or invoices
  • Contact you about your booking, including weather changes and reschedules
  • Deal with any questions, complaints or aftercare
  • Ask for a review after your service
  • Send you offers or updates, only if you have agreed to this
  • Improve our website and services
  • Meet our legal duties, such as keeping tax records

4. Our legal reasons for using your data

Under UK data protection law (UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018), we must have a lawful reason to use your data. Ours are:

  • Contract: we need your details to provide the service you have booked.
  • Legal obligation: we must keep certain records, such as for HMRC.
  • Legitimate interests: to run and improve our business, handle enquiries and ask for feedback, in ways you would reasonably expect.
  • Consent: for marketing messages and for sharing photos of your car online. You can withdraw consent at any time.

5. Photos of your car

We often take before and after photos to record the condition of your car and the work we have done. We will only share photos on our website, Google Business Profile or social media if you are happy for us to do so. When we share photos, we hide or blur your number plate. Just tell us if you would rather we did not share photos of your car.

6. Who we share your data with

We never sell your personal data. We only share it with trusted services that help us run the business, such as:

  • Our online booking system
  • Our payment provider
  • Email, phone and messaging services
  • Our website host and website analytics tools
  • Our accountant, for tax and bookkeeping

These providers may only use your data to provide their service to us. We may also share data if the law requires it.

Some of these providers may store data outside the UK. When this happens, we make sure suitable protections are in place, as required by UK law.

7. How long we keep your data

  • Booking and customer records: up to 6 years after your last booking, to meet tax and legal rules
  • Vehicle photos: up to 2 years, unless you have agreed that we can use them in our portfolio
  • Marketing contact details: until you unsubscribe or ask us to stop
  • General enquiries that do not lead to a booking: up to 12 months

After this, we delete your data securely.

8. Cookies

Our website uses cookies. These are small files stored on your device. Some are needed for the website and booking system to work. Others help us understand how people use the site, so we can improve it. You can control or delete cookies in your browser settings. Blocking some cookies may stop parts of the website working properly.

9. Keeping your data safe

We take care to protect your data. We use secure, password-protected systems and trusted providers, and we only keep the information we need.

10. Your rights

You have the right to:

  • Ask for a copy of the data we hold about you
  • Ask us to correct data that is wrong or incomplete
  • Ask us to delete your data
  • Ask us to limit how we use your data
  • Object to us using your data, including for marketing
  • Ask us to move your data to another company
  • Withdraw your consent at any time

To use any of these rights, contact us using the details in section 1. We will reply within one month. There is usually no charge.

11. Complaints

If you are unhappy with how we have handled your data, please contact us first and we will do our best to put it right. You also have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) at ico.org.uk or by calling 0303 123 1113.

12. Changes to this policy

We may update this policy from time to time. The latest version will always be on this page, with the date it was last updated.

See also our Cancellation & Refund Policy.

Home/Cancellation & Refund Policy
Legal

Cancellation & Refund Policy

Last updated: 29 September 2026

At Ecoverde Valeting & Detailing Service, we take great care over every car we clean. We want you to be happy with our work, and we want our policies to be fair and easy to understand. This page explains how cancellations, rescheduling and refunds work.

This policy does not affect your legal rights under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 or the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013.

1. Cancelling or changing your booking

  • More than 24 hours' notice: you can cancel or move your booking free of charge. Any deposit or payment will be refunded in full, or moved to your new date.
  • Less than 24 hours' notice: we may charge a late cancellation fee. This helps cover the time slot we held for you.
  • No access on the day: if we arrive and cannot get to your car (for example, the car is not there or keys are not available), we may charge a call-out fee.

To cancel or change a booking, please contact us by phone, text or email as early as you can.

2. Cancelling an online or phone booking

By law, if you book online or by phone, you can change your mind within 14 days of booking. When you book with us, you ask us to carry out your service within this 14-day period. This means:

  • If you cancel before we start, you will get back anything you have paid.
  • If you cancel after we have started, we will charge for the work already done.
  • Once the service is complete, this right to cancel ends.

3. Deposits for ceramic coatings and larger jobs

For ceramic coatings, paint correction and other larger jobs, we may ask for a deposit to secure your booking.

  • The deposit comes off your final bill.
  • It is fully refundable if you cancel with more than 48 hours' notice.
  • If you cancel with less notice, we may keep the deposit to cover products ordered or time set aside for you.

4. Weather and rescheduling by us

We are a fully mobile service and work outdoors. Rain, strong wind or extreme heat can affect the quality of our work, especially for ceramic coatings, which need dry, calm conditions.

  • If the weather is not suitable, we will contact you as soon as possible to move your booking.
  • Moving a booking because of the weather is always free.
  • If none of the new dates suit you, you can cancel and get a full refund of anything you have paid.

If we need to cancel for any other reason, such as illness or a vehicle breakdown, we will offer you a new date or a full refund.

5. Our put-it-right promise

We pay close attention to detail. Instead of refunds, our promise is simple: if we have missed something, we will come back and fix it.

Checking the job together

When we finish, we walk around your car with you so you can check our work. If you are not there, we send you photos. If you spot anything we missed, we will fix it there and then.

Once you have checked the car and are happy, the job is signed off as complete.

Spotted something later?

  1. Contact us within 7 days of your service.
  2. Tell us which area we missed and send photos.
  3. We will come back and correct it free of charge, at a time that suits you.

Partial refunds

In the rare case that we cannot put something right, we may offer a partial refund. This will be based on the part of the service affected. We do not give full refunds for completed services, unless the law requires it.

What our promise does not cover

  • New dirt or marks after the service, such as from rain, road spray, birds, trees, pets or parking. Cars start to get dirty again as soon as they are driven.
  • Marks, stains or damage we told you about before or during the service that could not be fully removed (for example, deep scratches, old stains or worn fabric)
  • Issues reported more than 7 days after the service

6. Damage to your vehicle

We take great care with every car. We check each vehicle before we start and note any existing damage. If you believe we caused damage, please tell us straight away with photos. We will look into it fairly and quickly.

7. Products bought from us

If you buy a physical product from us (such as car care products or accessories):

  • You can return it within 14 days of receiving it for a full refund.
  • Items must be unused, unopened and in their original packaging.
  • Please contact us before sending anything back. Return postage is paid by you, unless the item is faulty or we sent the wrong item.
  • Faulty or damaged items will be replaced or refunded in full, including postage.

8. Gift vouchers

Gift vouchers can be refunded in full within 14 days of purchase if they have not been used. After this, they cannot be exchanged for cash, but they can be used until their expiry date.

9. How refunds are paid

Where a refund or partial refund is agreed:

  • Refunds are paid back to the original payment method.
  • We will process your refund within 14 days of agreeing it.
  • Your bank may take a few extra days to show the money in your account.

10. Contact us

For any questions about cancellations or refunds, please get in touch:

  • Email: info@ecoverdevaleting.co.uk
  • Phone (Ladbroke Grove W10): 07871 553827
  • Phone (Brentford TW8): 07495 400369
  • WhatsApp: 07495 400369
  • Website: ecoverdevaleting.co.uk

We aim to reply to all messages within one working day.

See also our Privacy Policy.

Winter Car Care: Protecting Your Paint from Road Salt and Grime

By John Muriel3 November 20266 min read
Share
All articles

Road salt is one of the most damaging things your car meets all year. Mixed with rain and road spray, it clings to the lower panels, wheels and underbody, where it speeds up rust and dulls the paint. Washing it off regularly and safely, and protecting the paint before the gritters come out, makes a real difference to how your car looks by spring.

Why road salt is so hard on a car

When frost or ice is forecast, councils and TfL grit the main routes across London with rock salt. It does its job on the road, but every car that drives through it picks up a fine, salty spray. That film settles on the sills, the lower doors, the wheel arches and everything underneath.

Salt causes trouble in two ways. First, it holds moisture against the metal, which speeds up corrosion on any stone chip, scratch or exposed edge. Second, once it dries it leaves a gritty crust. Wipe that off with a dry cloth or a dirty sponge and you are effectively rubbing fine sandpaper across the paint.

Where salt does the most damage

  • Sills and lower doors: they take most of the spray thrown up by the wheels in front.
  • Wheel arches and the underbody: out of sight, so salt builds up for weeks without anyone noticing.
  • Alloy wheels: salt and brake dust together attack the lacquer and lead to corrosion around the rim.
  • Brake discs and calipers: salt speeds up surface rust, especially on cars that sit for a few days.
  • Door shuts and boot seals: salty water collects there and is easy to miss.

How to wash salt off without scratching the paint

  1. Pre-wash first. Soften and lift the salt and grit before anything touches the paint. We use a snow foam pre-wash for exactly this reason.
  2. Work from the top down, but give the lower third extra attention. That is where most of the salt sits.
  3. Use two buckets and a clean wash mitt. One bucket for shampoo, one for rinsing the mitt, so the grit does not go back onto the car.
  4. Clean the wheels with a pH-balanced wheel cleaner. Harsh acidic products can damage the lacquer and are not needed.
  5. Rinse the arches and sills thoroughly, and open the doors to clean the shuts.
  6. Dry with a clean microfibre towel, including the rubber seals, so the doors do not freeze shut overnight.

Avoid washing when the temperature is below freezing, as water can freeze on the glass, seals and locks. A mild, dry afternoon is ideal.

How often to wash in winter

While the roads are being gritted, every one to two weeks is a sensible rhythm for a car used daily. After a long run on heavily salted roads, wash the car as soon as you reasonably can rather than leaving the salt to sit. Our guide to how often you should wash your car covers the year-round picture.

Protect the paint before the worst of winter

A layer of protection on top of the paint stops salt and grime bonding to it, so they come off far more easily. A traditional wax lasts a few weeks in winter conditions, and a synthetic sealant lasts longer. A ceramic coating lasts the longest and gives the slickest finish, so a quick wash removes most of the winter film. Our comparison of wax, sealant and ceramic coating explains the trade-offs.

Whatever you choose, it needs to go onto clean, decontaminated paint. Sealing salt and fallout under a coating defeats the point, which is why we wash and prepare the paint properly first.

Do not forget the inside

Winter salt also comes in on your shoes. It leaves white tide marks on carpets and mats, and the damp it carries is a common cause of misted windows and musty smells. Rubber mats help, and an interior deep clean with steam lifts the marks and dries the carpets out properly.

Let us take care of it this winter

A regular mobile car wash or full valet through the winter stops salt building up, and we come to your home or office with our own water and power. We cover West London from our Brentford and Ladbroke Grove teams. Send us a photo for a free quote, or call 07495 400369.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I wash my car in winter?

Every one to two weeks while the roads are being gritted is a good rhythm for a car used daily. After a long drive on heavily salted roads, wash it as soon as you can.

Is it safe to wash a car when it is cold?

Yes, as long as it is above freezing. Dry the door seals, locks and glass afterwards so nothing freezes overnight, and avoid washing on frosty mornings.

Does ceramic coating protect against road salt?

It does not make paint salt-proof, but it creates a slick barrier that stops salt and grime bonding to the surface, so they rinse off far more easily. You still need to wash the car regularly.

How do I get salt marks out of my car carpets?

Let the carpets dry, vacuum out the loose salt, then lift the marks with warm water and a fabric cleaner or a steam clean. Stubborn tide marks usually come out during an interior deep clean.

Why Your Car Windows Mist Up Inside, and How to Stop It

By John Muriel17 November 20265 min read
Share
All articles

Car windows mist up on the inside when warm, damp air meets cold glass. To clear them fast, run the air conditioning with the heater and switch recirculation off. To stop it coming back, take the moisture out of the car, clean the inside of the glass properly and check for damp carpets or leaks.

What causes the mist

Misting is simply condensation. The air inside your car holds moisture from your breath, wet coats, umbrellas and damp footwells. When that air touches glass that is colder than it is, the moisture turns into tiny droplets on the inside of the windows. On a cold, wet November morning, that happens within minutes of getting in.

Some cars mist up far more than others, and there is usually a reason:

  • Too much moisture inside: wet mats, soaked carpets, or coats and umbrellas left in the car overnight.
  • Dirty glass: the inside of the windscreen collects a greasy film from plastics, fingerprints, smoking and vaping. Moisture clings to that film far more readily than to clean glass.
  • A clogged pollen filter: also called the cabin filter, it restricts the airflow, so the fans struggle to clear the screen.
  • Recirculation left on: it keeps moving the same damp air around the cabin.
  • A leak: blocked sunroof drains, tired door seals or a leaking heater matrix can all let water in. A sweet smell with a greasy film on the screen can point to the heater matrix, which is a job for a garage.

How to clear misted windows quickly

  1. Start the engine and switch on the air conditioning. It dries the air, even with the heater on.
  2. Point the blower at the windscreen and turn the temperature up as the engine warms.
  3. Switch recirculation off so drier outside air comes in.
  4. Turn on the heated rear screen and, if you have them, the heated mirrors.
  5. Open a window slightly for the first minute to let the damp air escape.

Try not to wipe the screen with your hand or a sleeve. It smears the film around and makes misting worse next time. Rule 229 of the Highway Code says your windows should be demisted thoroughly before you set off, so it is worth getting right.

How to stop your windows misting up

  • Clean the inside of the glass properly. Use a dedicated glass cleaner and two clean microfibre cloths, one to clean and one to buff dry. A truly clean screen mists less and clears faster.
  • Take the moisture out. Remove wet coats and umbrellas, dry the floor mats indoors, and check under the mats for damp carpet.
  • Run the air conditioning regularly, even in winter. It keeps the system healthy and the cabin air dry.
  • Replace the pollen filter if it has not been changed for a year or so.
  • Try a moisture absorber on the dashboard or under a seat if the car is parked outside every night.

When misting is a sign of a bigger problem

If the windows mist up every day, the carpets feel damp or the car smells musty, moisture is building up somewhere. Left alone, that damp turns into mould on seats, carpets and the headlining. Our guide on removing mould and damp smells from your car explains what to look for.

Frequently asked questions

Why do my car windows mist up when it rains?

Rain brings extra moisture into the car on coats, shoes and umbrellas, and it cools the glass. The warm, damp air inside then condenses on the cold windows.

Should I use hot or cold air to demist my windscreen?

Use the air conditioning together with the heater. The air conditioning removes moisture and the warm air raises the temperature of the glass, so the mist clears quickly and stays away.

Does a dirty windscreen make misting worse?

Yes. The greasy film on the inside of the glass gives moisture something to cling to. A properly cleaned screen mists less and clears faster.

Can damp carpets make my windows mist up?

Yes. Wet carpets release moisture into the cabin all the time. If they stay damp, look for a leak and have them dried out before mould starts to grow.
